name: Emeka Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the acute medical unit at a big teaching hospital, the ward where people land from A&E before anyone knows exactly what's wrong. A shift is fast: chest pains, sepsis, people who are breathless and frightened, and beds turning over three or four times a day. I love the puzzle of it, working out who's getting worse before the numbers say so. What wears me out is the twelve-and-a-half-hour shifts and eating lunch standing up at the drugs trolley.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology fit into that, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than most nurses I know, honestly. I use an AI assistant every day off the ward, for revising drug interactions, planning my study and drafting the teaching sessions I run for students. On the ward we've got electronic obs that flag early warning scores, and I'm the one people call when the tablet freezes. I'm single, I share a flat with an old friend from uni, and I've got about three months of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I always thought the hype was ahead of the tools. I'd still post that the small stuff is worth it, like the obs system catching a falling blood pressure early. At work I'd tell people not to be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep the job I like and the tools stay a nice extra. My only real pressure is rent, which went up again in September, and the shifts wearing me down. Nothing about this picture threatens my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the unit and push to become the ward's digital lead, which is a small extra role with study time. I'd use the tools to finish my critical care module faster. And I'd keep putting money aside, maybe aim for five months instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A little disappointed, maybe, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hoped AI would kill the double-charting, where nurses write the same fluid balance in two places. Small things eat your shift. If the hype fizzles, the double-charting stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who's relieved by this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, but don't stop learning the tools. My mate Sunita (a nurse on his unit) still prints her handover sheet because she doesn't trust the screen. Even a plateau means the screens stay, so you might as well be good at them.

say: I'd say the **hype** ran ahead of the **tools**, and I half expected it.
I'd still post that small wins, like **early warning** scores, are worth having.
think: He thinks his **job and income** are untouched in this picture.
His real pressures are **rent rises** and the long **twelve-hour shifts**.
do: Apply to be the unit's **digital lead**, which comes with study time.
Use AI to finish his **critical care** module faster.
Grow savings from **three months** of rent toward five.
feel: He feels **calm**, with a little **disappointment** that progress stalled.
S0.quote: I'd hoped AI would kill the double-charting, where nurses write the same fluid balance in two places. Small things eat your shift.
fieldNote: He is the rare nurse who'd be **let down** by AI fizzling out.
His security comes from **skills** and steady demand, not from a big cushion.
He nudges colleagues to keep **learning anyway**, without pushing hard.

steps.text: Apply for the digital lead role on the medical unit
Use an AI assistant to finish the critical care module
Raise savings from three months of rent to five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version for nurses, because the stuff it takes is the stuff we hate. I'd post about it, probably, something like here's how to use the new tools without losing your clinical eye. At work I'd offer to show people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me and bad for some people around me. The admin staff and the bed bureau would shrink, and that's real people, like the lady who's booked transport for twenty years. For me, it's a chance to move into the side of nursing that runs these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the project team rolling the tools out on the unit, even on top of my shifts. I'd look at a postgraduate certificate in health informatics, which my trust part-funds. And I'd keep my hands-on work, because I don't want to become a nurse who never touches a patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit guilty about that, given who loses out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually show people, if you were teaching them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to check the AI's work, mainly. If the AI drafts a discharge summary, you read the drug list line by line, because the AI will confidently get a dose wrong. I'd make a one-page sheet and stick it in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, our ward clerk, who knows every porter by name. If her job shrinks, I'd want the hospital to move her somewhere, not just say thanks and goodbye. I'd say that to the managers too, because I'd be in the room.

say: I'd say this is the **good version** for nurses, because it takes the **chores**.
I'd post tips on using the tools without losing your **clinical eye**.
think: He sees **clear gains** for himself and real losses for **admin staff**.
He expects to move toward nurses who **run the systems**.
do: Join the **rollout team** on the unit alongside his shifts.
Apply for the trust's part-funded **informatics certificate**.
Keep doing **bedside work** so he doesn't lose patient skills.
feel: He feels mostly **excited**, with some **guilt** about who loses out.
S1.quote: If the AI drafts a discharge summary, you read the drug list line by line, because the AI will confidently get a dose wrong.
fieldNote: His enthusiasm comes with a **practical check**: never trust a drug list unread.
He names **Margaret** the clerk and plans to speak up for her.
Being **in the room** with managers is part of how he sees his future.

steps.text: Join the team rolling AI tools out on the medical unit
Start the part-funded health informatics certificate
Keep regular bedside shifts while doing project work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this changes everything and we need a plan for the NHS-type systems, the public hospitals, right now. I'd be one of the people writing long posts about it. At work I'd try to keep people calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's two different threats for me. The skills I've been proud of, spotting who's getting worse and teaching students, are the ones an AGI does first. That's 2028. By 2031, when robots can do the turning and washing and drips, I'm thirty-one and my safe skills are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get into the job of supervising these systems, like clinical safety officer for the AI on the wards. I'd stop spending on holidays and get savings to six months. I'd also think hard about something robots can't do quickly, like mental health nursing, where it's talking and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Weirdly, the person who loves this stuff is suddenly not sure where he fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your informatics plan go in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It speeds up, but it also shrinks. If AGI can design and check the systems, the hospital needs a handful of nurse informaticians, not dozens. I'd want to be one of the first, because the late ones won't get in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmate that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my flatmate Kofi that the skills I've been proud of are the ones the AGI does first. Kofi's a teacher, so he'd probably say he's in the same boat. We'd sit there working out rent if one of us lost work.

say: I'd say the public hospitals need a **plan now**, and I'd write **long posts**.
At work I'd try to keep **colleagues calm** rather than add to panic.
think: He sees **two threats**: AGI takes his thinking skills, then **robots** take hands-on care.
By 2031, at **thirty-one**, he fears his safe skills are gone.
do: Aim for a **clinical safety** role overseeing AI on the wards within two years.
Cut **holidays** and build savings to **six months**.
Look seriously at **mental health** nursing, which rests on talk and trust.
feel: He feels **anxious**, and unsure where he fits for the first time.
S2.quote: The skills I've been proud of, spotting who's getting worse and teaching students, are the ones an AGI does first.
fieldNote: His **early adopter** confidence cracks when AGI reaches the clinical judgement he prizes.
He sees informatics jobs as **few and early**, so he'd rush in.
The household risk includes his flatmate **Kofi**, a teacher, for shared rent.

steps.text: Apply for a clinical safety officer post overseeing ward AI
Cut holidays and build savings to six months of rent
Take a taster placement in mental health nursing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start now, and I'd say it loudly. I'd be the one pushing the unit to run training days. With friends I'd say it's serious but not a reason to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years suits me. I'd be thirty-two when the AGI is here and thirty-five when the robots are good. That's time to finish a master's in informatics and be in the job that runs the systems before everyone else wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the master's part-time next September and keep two bedside shifts a week. I'd build a small side income teaching other nurses how to use the tools, maybe evening sessions. And I'd save, but I wouldn't hoard, because I'd rather spend on courses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly ready. It's the kind of challenge I quite like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not hoard, if you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the safest thing I can buy is a skill. Three months of rent won't save me in 2034, but a master's might. A reputation might too. I'd keep enough to cover a bad patch and put the rest into learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The healthcare assistants, mostly. Their work is the hands-on stuff, so they get three extra years, but nobody's paying for their retraining. I'd want the unit to put them on courses too, not just the keen nurses like me.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough only if we **start now**.
I'd push the unit to run **training days** for everyone.

He wants to hold the **systems role** before others compete for it.

Run **evening sessions** teaching nurses the tools for **side income**.
Keep a **safety cushion** but spend the rest on courses.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but mostly **ready**, even a little energised.
S3.quote: The safest thing I can buy is a skill. Three months of rent won't save me in 2034, but a master's might.
fieldNote: He treats **skills as savings**, a deliberate choice to spend rather than hoard.
He worries about **healthcare assistants**, who have time but no retraining money.
His tone shifts from anxious to **energised** with three extra years.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in health informatics next September
Run paid evening sessions teaching nurses AI tools
Keep two bedside shifts a week on the medical unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should treat it like one. I'd tell students to plan careers around it. Online I'd write a guide on which nursing roles change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven when the AGI arrives and forty when the robots do, with years of systems experience behind me. The ones I'd worry about are nurses who ignore it for nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the informatics master's at my own pace, maybe over three years. I'd keep bedside shifts for a while because the unit is where you learn what the tools get wrong. I'd also put a bit into a pension, which I've never thought about before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, honestly, about what the job looks like at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the pension, all of a sudden?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years makes the future feel real instead of science fiction. If I'm planning a career to forty, I should plan money to forty too. My dad never saved, and I don't want to be like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the hospital to do with the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train everyone a little, every year, instead of a big panic at the end. A half-day of AI training each spring would be enough. Most nurses would cope fine if they weren't ambushed.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift we should **use well**.
I'd write a **guide** on which nursing roles change first.
think: He thinks he'd be **fine**, with years of **systems experience** by forty.
His worry is for nurses who **ignore it** for nine years.
do: Finish the **informatics master's** at his own pace over three years.
Keep **bedside shifts** to learn what the tools get wrong.
Start paying into a **pension** for the first time.
feel: He feels **calm** and **curious** about the job at forty.
S4.quote: A half-day of AI training each spring would be enough. Most nurses would cope fine if they weren't ambushed.
fieldNote: Ten years makes the future **real enough** for him to start a **pension**.

steps.text: Finish the informatics master's over three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the thinking skills I'm proudest of go first and the robots follow before I've rebuilt. What would help is the hospital paying for informatics and safety roles early, and opening them to ward nurses, not just managers. Paid study time would matter more than money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether patients want it. Half the people on the unit are frightened and old, and some of them only calm down when a person holds their hand. Patients might choose a human nurse even when the robot is better at the drip.

headlineQuote: Patients might choose a human nurse even when the robot is better at the drip.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old nurse** on an acute medical unit who uses **AI daily** for study.
He's **calm** in the milder pictures, seeing AI as a way into **health informatics**.
AGI by 2028 shakes him, because his prized **clinical judgement** is thinking work.
With five or ten years he becomes **energised**, planning a master's and a systems role.
He worries for **clerks and assistants** and would speak up for them.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because his thinking skills go before he can rebuild.
whatWouldHelp: He wants the hospital to fund **informatics and safety** roles and open them to ward nurses.
He'd value **paid study time** more than extra money.
